walkthroughs.body_html:
World Religions Option — a core area of A-Level Religious Studies.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

World Religions Option brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with World Religions Option.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What is substance dualism about mind and body?
options: Substance dualism is the belief that humans have two personalities.
Substance dualism means men and women are different.
The view (associated with Descartes) that mind and body are two distinct kinds of substance — a non-physical mind interacting with a physical body.
Orthodox Judaism is a different religion from Reform Judaism.

mcqs.q: What does natural law theory base morality on?
options: Orthodox Judaism is a different religion from Reform Judaism.
Natural law means whatever happens in nature is morally right.
Human nature and reason — there are objective purposes (telos) built into humans which reason can discover, generating universal moral precepts.
Natural law is the same thing as the laws of physics.

mcqs.q: How does Reform Judaism differ from Orthodox Judaism?
options: Orthodox Judaism is a different religion from Reform Judaism.
Substance dualism means men and women are different.

Reform Judaism treats Jewish law (halakhah) as evolving and not strictly binding, embraces modernity, and grants gender equality; Orthodox Judaism holds halakhah as divinely given and binding in detail, with traditional practice maintained.
Reform Jews don't believe in God and Orthodox Jews do.
